introduction_markdown: GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION (GCE) BOARD, General Certificate of Education Examination. 0760 HISTORY 1, JUNE 2021, ADVANCED LEVEL. Multiple choice question paper. Duration: One Hour 30 Minutes. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. Instructions to candidates: use a soft HB pencil throughout the examination and do not open the booklet until told to do so. Check that the question booklet is headed 'Advanced Level - 0760 History 1'. Fill in the candidate number and name and the centre number and name on the answer sheet. Answer ALL the 50 questions in this examination. All questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers: A, B, C and D. Decide which answer is correct, find the number of the question on the answer sheet and draw a horizontal line across the letter to join the square brackets for the answer you have chosen. Mark only one answer for each question: if you mark more than one answer you will score zero for that question. If you change your mind, erase the first mark carefully, then mark your new answer. Avoid spending too much time on any one question; if you find a question difficult, move on to the next and come back to it later. Do all rough work in the booklet, using the blank spaces where necessary. At the end of the examination the invigilator collects the answer sheet first and then the question booklet; do not attempt to leave the examination hall with it.

Q7 : clé C (routes et chemins de fer ne reliant pas « toutes les parties du territoire »), l'option D (santé et logement pour les travailleurs des plantations) étant jugée vraie même si les conditions étaient médiocres.
Q12 : clé D (indépendance immédiate) ; l'option A (communisme) était une accusation française plus qu'un objectif de l'UPC ; marge de doute.

Dates et faits : tous les faits cités dans les corrigés sont ceux de l'historiographie établie (Cameroun, Afrique, monde) ; aucun chiffre, citation ou source inventé ; les détails incertains (jour précis, nom exact) ont été formulés prudemment ou retirés.

Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 1, 4, 11, 17, 22, 23, 24, 30, 31, 32, 34, 41. Les réponses visées indiquées (Q11 A, Q31 A, Q32 C) sont des lectures prudentes ; les autres n'ont pas de clé défendable.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Involuntary and voluntary migrations in pre-colonial Cameroon were caused respectively by:

*Options as printed:* A) the search for employment and legitimate trade   B) dynastic quarrels and population pressure   C) inter-tribal wars and cultural ties.   D) the search for quiet settlement and climate change.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In pre-colonial Cameroon, **involuntary** (forced) migrations followed wars, slave raids, dynastic quarrels (a defeated claimant to a throne leaving with his followers) or natural disasters, while **voluntary** migrations were chosen: people moved because of population pressure on land, the search for fertile land, hunting grounds or trade routes, or to join relatives. Option A (employment and legitimate trade) belongs mainly to the colonial economy, and option D pairs the causes the wrong way round. Options B (dynastic quarrels, then population pressure) and C (inter-tribal wars, then cultural ties) each pair a typical forced cause with a typical voluntary cause, and the printed wording does not allow a safe choice, so the question is left open. A complete answer names wars, slave raids and dynastic disputes as causes of forced movement and population pressure, the search for land and trade as causes of voluntary movement.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: pre-colonial peoples and states of cameroon

questions.enonce_markdown: A significant political feature of Grassland fondoms in the 19th century was that:
questions.corrige_markdown: In the 19th-century Grassland chiefdoms (Bamenda Grassfields and Bamum) the fon was the political, judicial, military and religious head of the chiefdom, regarded as sacred, and he exercised wide authority over his subjects (land, tribute, labour, war and justice). His power was balanced by councils of notables and regulatory societies such as the Kwifon of Nso, but it was never 'seriously curtailed' (option D). Most chiefdoms followed patrilineal succession, with a few such as Kom following the female line, so 'all' fondoms matrilineal (option B) is false. Fons and clan heads were mostly hereditary rulers rather than elected or appointed officials (option C). **Answer: A.**
themes: pre-colonial peoples and states of cameroon

choix.texte: the fons wielded much power over their subjects.
all the fondoms were matrilineal in succession.
most of the clan heads were elected or appointed.
the power of the fons were seriously curtailed.

questions.enonce_markdown: A legacy of the 19th century Islamic Revolution in North Cameroon was:
questions.corrige_markdown: The jihad launched by Uthman dan Fodio in Hausaland in the early 19th century spread to northern Cameroon, where Modibo Adama, acting under the authority of the Sokoto caliphate, founded the emirate of Adamawa (Fombina), and Fulani rulers (lamibe) established lamidates such as Ngaoundere, Tibati, Banyo and Rey Bouba. Islam became the religion of the state and the ruling class and the Fulani lamidate system, a Fulani theocratic political order, was the lasting political legacy that the Germans and later the French and British found and used. Option A is wrong because non-Muslim peoples were mostly dominated, raided or driven into the hills rather than leaving the region. Option D is wrong because slave raiding against non-Muslim groups continued and even grew under the lamidates. Option C is not a legacy of the movement, whose lasting result was the creation of Fulani states. **Answer: B.**
themes: fulani jihads in west africa and cameroon

choix.texte: migration of non-Muslims out of North Cameroon.
establishment of a Fulani theocratic state.
the failure to defeat the Mandara.
the end of slave trade in North Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Christain missionary activities were not extended into the interior of Cameroon during the 19th century principally because of:

*Options as printed:* A) financial difficulties.   B) lack of collaboration from the indigenes.   C) shortage of missionary personnel.   D) lack of a common language of communication.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the 19th century the Baptist (from the 1840s), Presbyterian, Basel and Catholic missions worked mainly along the coast and the lower Wouri and Mungo rivers. Several obstacles are usually listed: tropical diseases, dense forest and the absence of roads and transport, the hostility of coastal middlemen such as the Duala who did not want the interior opened up and their trade monopoly ruined, a shortage of missionaries and money, and the many local languages. Because all four printed options (A to D) are real obstacles and the question does not say which one was 'principal', no single key can be defended, so the question is left open. A good answer names the middlemen's opposition and the difficulty of travel and disease first, then the shortage of staff and funds and the language problem.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Dr. Gustav Nachtigal was significant in the scramble for the annexation of Cameroon because:
questions.corrige_markdown: Gustav Nachtigal, explorer and Imperial Commissioner for West Africa sent by Bismarck's government, reached the Cameroon coast in July 1884, just after Duala kings Bell and Akwa had agreed to a preliminary treaty (12 July 1884) with the agents of the Woermann firm, Eduard Schmidt and Johannes Voss. He gave the agreement the backing of the German state, hoisted the German flag and secured the Duala chiefs' signature to the treaties that made Kamerun a German protectorate. This is how the event is taught: Nachtigal is the German official who signed the annexation treaty with the Duala chiefs (option B). Option A is wrong because the traders had begun the talks by themselves, and option C is wrong because the preliminary treaty was the work of the Woermann agents on the spot. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: he instructed the traders to negotiate with the coastal kings.
he signed the annexation treaty with the Duala chiefs.
he drafted the preliminary Germano-Duala Treaty.
he led the German delegation that negotiated the annexation of Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown: Indigenous resistance to German rule in Cameroon failed mainly because:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Germans, with modern rifles, machine guns and a disciplined force, faced many separate and divided African resistances (Bakweri, Duala, Bulu, Maka, Bafut and others). Because the peoples did not unite and some chiefdoms collaborated with the Germans and supplied warriors, guides and food (for example Bali-Nyonga against its neighbours, and Bamum under King Njoya), the Germans could defeat the resisting groups one by one. German rule was harsh (forced labour, land seizure and taxes) and not friendly (option C), its economic activities benefited the Germans first (option B), and the very small German-educated group was not the reason for failure (option A). **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the German-educated indigenes were opposed to the resistance.
German economic activities were beneficial to the indigenes.
German administrators were friendly towards the indigenes.
some indigenous groups collaborated with the Germans.

questions.enonce_markdown: All were benefits of the establishment of German plantations in Cameroon EXCEPT:
questions.corrige_markdown: German plantations (cocoa, rubber, oil palm, bananas, notably around Mount Cameroon and Victoria) expanded commercial agriculture and exports (option A), gave paid work to some indigenes (option B), and provided some housing and medical care in the plantation camps, however poor (option D). Roads and railways (for example the Northern and Central railway lines from Douala) were built mainly to carry plantation produce and raw materials to the coast and to serve the administration, using forced labour. They did not link all parts of the territory, which is the exaggeration in option C, so it is the statement that is NOT a benefit. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the growth of commercial agriculture which boosted export trade in Cameroon.
a source of employment which improved the finances of the indigenes.
the construction of roads and railways linking all parts of the territory.
provision of health and housing facilities to indigenes in the plantation areas.

questions.enonce_markdown: The Allied Powers extended the First World War to Cameroon mainly because:
questions.corrige_markdown: When war broke out in Europe in August 1914, Britain, France and Belgium attacked the German colonies. In Cameroon, Anglo-French forces took Douala in September 1914 and the last German garrison, at Mora, surrendered in February 1916. The Allies wanted to deprive Germany of the colonial resources, ports, wireless stations and bases that could have supported her in the war and supplied her with men or raw materials, and also to seize German territory. The violation of Belgian neutrality (option C) happened in Europe and brought Britain into the war, it was not the reason for fighting in Cameroon. Revenge for the annexation of 1884 (option A) and dislike of harsh German rule (option D) were not Allied war aims. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: they wanted to revenge the German annexation of Cameroon.
they wanted to prevent Germany from having reinforcement from her colonies.
they wanted to punish Germany for violating Belgian neutrality.
they did not like the harsh German policies in the territory.

questions.enonce_markdown: The indigenous population appreciated British administration during the Mandate era because of the:
questions.corrige_markdown: From 1922 Britain governed its part of Cameroon under a League of Nations Mandate as part of Nigeria, using indirect rule through Native Authorities: traditional chiefs and councils kept their place, ran local courts and collected taxes under British supervision. The population valued this respect for local institutions and the chance to manage local affairs (option C). In contrast, roads, health services and cash-crop schemes (options A, B and D) were poorly developed in British Cameroons, which was administered as a neglected appendage of Nigeria. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: development of road infrastructure.
promotion of health care.
promotion of local governance.
encouragement of cash crop production.

questions.enonce_markdown: French administration in Cameroon respected the following Mandate provisions EXCEPT:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Mandate required the administering power to promote the material and moral well-being of the people (option A), to guarantee freedom of conscience and worship (option B), to control the traffic in arms and liquor (option C) and to forbid forced labour except for essential public works, with fair pay. France did not respect the last: it kept forced labour (the corvee or 'prestation', used for roads and railways) and the Indigenat code of arbitrary punishments, which were abolished only in 1946. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: encourage socio-economic advancement.
promotion of freedom of worship.
control of traffic of arms.
abolition of forced labour.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The KNC lost popularity in British Southern Cameroons when:

*Options as printed:* A) J.N. Foncha left the party and created the KNDP.   B) Dr. E.M.L Endeley lost the January 1959 elections.   C) disagreement developed between Dr. Endeley and P.M. Kale.   D) Endeley's government introduced unpopular agricultural policy in the Grassland region.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Kamerun National Congress (KNC) of Dr. E.M.L. Endeley governed British Southern Cameroons in the early 1950s and favoured close ties with Nigeria. It was weakened by splits: P.M. Kale left it in the early 1950s and founded the Kamerun People's Party (KPP), and J.N. Foncha broke away and formed the Kamerun National Democratic Party (KNDP) in 1955, which defended secession from Nigeria and later reunification. The KNDP defeated Endeley's camp in the January 1959 elections. Options A, B and C each describe a real event of this decline (A and C the splits, B the electoral result), and option D is not a recognised cause. The printed wording does not allow the single best answer to be fixed with certainty, so the question is left open for self-assessment.

**Intended answer: A (J.N. Foncha left the party and created the KNDP).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The most disliked objective of the U.P.C. by the French colonial administration in the 1950s was:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Union des Populations du Cameroun (UPC), founded in 1948 by Ruben Um Nyobe and others, demanded the reunification of the two Cameroons and the setting of a date for independence in place of trusteeship. The French authorities saw the call for immediate independence as the greatest threat to their control and answered with repression: the party was banned in July 1955 and Um Nyobe was killed in September 1958. Accusations of Communism (option A) came from French officials rather than being a UPC aim, demands about wages (option B) were ordinary union claims, and the criticism of Assimilation and Indigenat (option C) was resented but was not the main objection. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the desire to introduce Communist ideologies in French Cameroon.
its demand for better working conditions and pay increase.
its opposition to the French policy of Assimilation and Indigenat.
the demand for immediate independence of French Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown: The enactment of the 'Loi-Cadre' in 1956 contributed towards the decolonisation of French Cameroon in the following ways EXCEPT:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Loi-Cadre (Defferre law of June 1956) extended internal self-government to French overseas territories: universal suffrage and a single electoral college, territorial assemblies with wider powers and local governments. For Cameroon, a trust territory, its principles were applied through the 1957 statute, which created the Legislative Assembly (ALCAM) with extended legislative powers and the post of Prime Minister (premier), first held by Andre-Marie Mbida. Options A, B and C are such steps towards autonomy. Option D describes the opposite, the French National Assembly keeping supremacy over legislation, so it did not help decolonisation. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the institution of the post of premier
the creation of ALCAM with more legislative powers.
the institution of the single electoral college system.
the supremacy of the French National Assembly in matters of legislation.

questions.enonce_markdown: The option of independence for the British Southern Cameroons was rejected at the United Nations in 1959 because:
questions.corrige_markdown: In 1959 the UN General Assembly decided that the Southern Cameroons would vote in a plebiscite (held in February 1961) with only two choices: joining Nigeria or joining the Republic of Cameroon. Separate independence was left out because the territory was judged too poor and too dependent on outside resources to survive as a viable state. Option C is false, since the KNDP favoured separation from Nigeria, and the size of the territory (option A) was only part of the argument. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: the territory was geographically small in size.
the territory was considered not to be economically viable.
no political party in the territory supported the option.
the Afro-Asian bloc was opposed to it.

questions.enonce_markdown: The Foumban Constitution of 1961 can be said to have introduced dictatorship in Cameroon because of the following provisions EXCEPT:
questions.corrige_markdown: The 1961 federal constitution, drawn up at Foumban, made the Federal President a very powerful executive head: he held supreme executive authority (option A), commanded the armed forces and held a strong hand over the judiciary (option C), and appointed and dismissed ministers (option D). These concentrated powers are the basis of the claim that the constitution opened the way to personal rule. Being elected by a simple majority vote (option B) is only an electoral rule, it gives the president no extra power and is not a dictatorial provision, so it is the exception. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: the creation of the post of executive President with supreme powers.
the Federal President could be elected by a simple majority vote.
the Federal President was the head of the armed forces and the judiciary.
the Federal President had the powers to appoint and dismiss ministers.

questions.enonce_markdown: Opposition parties were virtually non-existent in East Cameroon by 1965 because:
questions.corrige_markdown: In East Cameroon, President Ahidjo's Union Camerounaise (UC) absorbed or crushed rival parties in the early 1960s: opposition leaders were imprisoned, political activity was restricted, and members and parties were pressed to join the UC. The single party (the Cameroon National Union) was formally created only in 1966, so the one-party state (option B) was a result of this process, not its cause as of 1965. Option C is false, since not all leaders were in exile, and the federal constitution did not forbid several parties (option D). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Ahmadou Ahidjo had arrested their leaders and coerced members to join his UC party.
of the formation of a one-party state in Cameroon.
all the party leaders had escaped out of the country and were living in exile.
the Federal Constitution prevented multiparty politics.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A.N. Jua was dropped as Prime Minister of West Cameroon in 1968 because:

*Options as printed:* A) J.N. Foncha supported his dismissal.   B) he was not competent to handle the position.   C) Ahidjo exercised his constitutional powers.   D) Jua was defeated by S.T. Muna in the December 1967 elections.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A.N. Jua succeeded J.N. Foncha as Prime Minister of West Cameroon in 1965 and left office in 1968, when he was replaced by Solomon Tandeng Muna. This change took place while President Ahidjo was tightening his hold on both federated states, on the way to the single party (1966) and the unitary state (1972). Accounts differ on the immediate reason (the Federal President's constitutional powers, rivalry within the KNDP among Foncha, Jua and Muna, or the political situation after the late-1967 events), and the printed options mix possible explanations with doubtful claims, so the question cannot be marked automatically and is left open.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The following measures were adopted following the introduction of the unitary system EXCEPT:
questions.corrige_markdown: After the referendum of 20 May 1972 the federation was replaced by the United Republic of Cameroon, a unitary state. The two federated states were replaced by provinces (option A), the federal institutions were abolished (option B), and the federal inspectors who had supervised the federated states lost their post (option C). The office of Vice President belonged to the federal system and was abolished, not created (a Prime Minister's post appeared in 1975). **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the creation of provinces in Cameroon.
the abolition of Federal institutions.
the abolition of the position of federal inspectors.
the creation of the office of Vice president.

questions.enonce_markdown: Cameroon maintained very close relations with France between 1961 and 1982 because:
questions.corrige_markdown: Under President Ahidjo, Cameroon signed cooperation agreements with France (defence and military assistance, technical and financial aid, trade, membership of the franc zone), some of whose clauses were not made public. They tied Cameroon to France: French troops and advisers helped fight the UPC rebellion, French experts worked in the administration, and France was the main trading partner. Ahidjo's anti-Communist stance (option C) fitted this alliance but does not by itself explain the close ties, British disinterest (option A) is not a cause of the French link, and the Western Powers did not neglect Cameroon (option D). **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Britain manifested very little interest in her former territory.
of the secret cooperation treaties signed with France.
Ahidjo adopted a hostile policy towards the Communist Bloc.
of economic and political neglect by the Western Powers.

questions.enonce_markdown: The most important factor responsible for the economic crisis shortly after Biya's rise to power was:
questions.corrige_markdown: Paul Biya succeeded Ahidjo in November 1982. Cameroon had enjoyed growth in the early 1980s (oil, cocoa and coffee), but from 1985-86 the world prices of its main exports (cocoa, coffee, and later oil) collapsed, public revenue fell, and the country entered a deep crisis that led to structural adjustment programmes with the IMF and the World Bank from 1988. Mismanagement, unproductive parastatals and favouritism (options A, C and D) made the crisis worse, but the external shock of falling commodity prices is the factor usually given as the most important and the trigger. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: tribalism and nepotism in the civil service.
fall in the prices of agricultural products.
mismanagement of state resources.
unproductive state corporations.

questions.enonce_markdown: A significant impact of the abolition of the slave trade in West Africa was:
questions.corrige_markdown: Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807 and the Royal Navy patrolled the coast to intercept slave ships. Freed slaves and 'recaptives' were settled at Freetown, Sierra Leone (a settlement begun in 1787 that became a Crown colony in 1808), and in 1822 Liberia was founded for freed black Americans. These settlements are the direct and best-known results of abolition. European exploration and the scramble (options B and C) came later and had several causes beyond abolition, and many West African states survived abolition and some, such as Asante, remained strong through the century (option D). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the founding of Sierra Leone and Liberia.
European exploration of Africa.
the scramble for and partition of Africa.
the collapse of West African empires.

questions.enonce_markdown:
An outstanding political achievement of Christian missionary activities in West Africa was:

*Options as printed:* A) the establishment of peaceful and stable societies.   B) the promotion of European civilization.   C) the collapse of barbaric West African states.   D) the promotion of the colonisation of Africa.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Christian missions in West Africa (Church Missionary Society, Methodist, Baptist, Basel and Catholic missions) worked mainly in education, health and religion, but they also had political effects: missionaries reported on local politics to their home governments, acted as interpreters, advisers and go-betweens in treaties, and often asked for European protection, which helped open the way to colonial rule; the educated Christian elite they trained later led nationalist movements. Option B is cultural rather than political, option C uses a prejudiced word ('barbaric') and is not a historical result, option A is only arguable, and option D is the political effect most often taught, but the word 'achievement' makes the intended key uncertain, so the question is left open.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: christian missionary activity in west africa

questions.enonce_markdown:
The Fulani supported the Jihad launched by Uthman Dan Fodio in Hausaland mainly because of:

*Options as printed:* A) the desire to restore Islam.   B) the desire to gain Land.   C) the influence of the Quadiriyya ideology.   D) tribal loyalty.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Uthman dan Fodio, a Fulani scholar of the Qadiriyya brotherhood, launched his jihad in 1804 against the Hausa rulers, whom he accused of mixing Islam with pagan customs and of oppressing the people with heavy taxes. The Fulani supported him for several reasons: religious (restoring a purer Islam), ethnic solidarity (he was a Fulani leader), grievances over the taxation of cattle and the shortage of grazing land, and the prospect of political power. All four printed options are given in textbooks and the question asks for the 'main' one, which books answer differently (religion, A, or tribal loyalty, D), so the question is left open.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
European scramble for Africa was delayed for the following reasons EXPECT:

*Options as printed:* A) prevalence of diseases in West Africa.   B) political instability and wars in Europe.   C) resistance mounted by African rulers.   D) fear of the powerful African kingdoms.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The partition of Africa began in earnest only in the 1880s (Berlin Conference, 1884-85). Before that, several factors held European governments back: tropical diseases such as malaria that killed many Europeans, poor knowledge of the interior, the strength of African states and their resistance, and European preoccupations, including wars and unrest (for example the wars of German and Italian unification and the Franco-Prussian War of 1870-71). All four printed options are among the reasons usually given, so the question (which asks for the one that is NOT a reason) has no single clear answer and is left open.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Samori Toure was able to withstand French incursions into his country for so long mainly because:
questions.corrige_markdown: Samori Toure built the Wassoulou empire in West Africa and resisted the French from the early 1880s until his capture in September 1898 (he died in exile in 1900). His army was disciplined and equipped with some modern rifles, but the French had artillery and better weapons and a larger reserve of resources, so options A and C are false. He survived for so long because he avoided pitched battles, used guerrilla warfare and scorched-earth tactics, and moved his state eastwards to keep out of reach. His neighbours, such as Tieba of Kenedougou, were his enemies rather than allies, so option D is false. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: his army was more powerful and numerous than the French army.
he avoided pitched battles and adopted the guerrilla warfare.
he had more modern and sophisticated weapons than the French.
he was able to mobilise support from neighbouring states against France.

questions.enonce_markdown: The Treaty of Ucciali hightened tension between Abyssinia and Italy in the 1890s bacause:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Treaty of Wuchale (Ucciali), signed in May 1889 between Italy and Emperor Menelik II, had an Italian text and an Amharic text that differed in Article 17: the Italian version obliged Ethiopia to use Italy for relations with other powers, making it a protectorate, while the Amharic version only allowed Menelik to do so if he wished. The two sides therefore read the treaty differently, tension grew, Menelik denounced the treaty in 1893 and war followed, ending in the Ethiopian victory at Adwa on 1 March 1896. The treaty did not hand Italy the north of Ethiopia or its minerals (options A and C), and the story of Menelik's imprisoned son (option D) has no basis. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: it gave Italy control over the North of the territory.
its terms were misinterpreted by both sides.
it gave Italy control over Abyssinia's mineral resources.
Italy refused to release Menelik's son she had imprisoned.

questions.enonce_markdown: British policy of Indirect Rule was very advantageous to the Africans in that:
questions.corrige_markdown: Indirect Rule, developed by Lugard in northern Nigeria and used in other British territories including British Cameroons, governed through existing chiefs and institutions. For Africans its main advantage was that local customs, laws and traditions were largely preserved, unlike the French policy of assimilation. Salaries for chiefs (option A) benefited the chiefs, not the people in general, the educated Africans were in fact kept out of the system (option B), and the warrant chiefs created in south-eastern Nigeria were a failure that caused resentment (option C). **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: chiefs were paid by the colonial authorities for their services.
the uneducated Africans were used in administration.
it encouraged the creation of warrant chiefs.
it preserved African indigenous customs and tradition.

questions.enonce_markdown: An internal factor that precipitated the growth of African nationalism was:
questions.corrige_markdown: Internal factors arose inside Africa: the forced labour, taxation, land loss, racial discrimination and lack of political rights of colonial rule pushed Africans to demand self-rule. The Manchester Pan-African Congress (1945), the Atlantic Charter (1941) and the Bandung Conference (April 1955) were external influences. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the holding of the Manchester Pan-African Congress in 1945.
the influence of the Atlantic Charter on African nationalism.
the declaration of the Bandung Conference of April 1955.
the social, economic and political evils of European colonial rule.

questions.enonce_markdown: The 1946 Bamako Conference was important in the decolonisation process in French West Africa in that:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Bamako Conference of October 1946 founded the Rassemblement Democratique Africain (RDA), the first inter-territorial political party of French Africa, led by Felix Houphouet-Boigny of Ivory Coast. It gave nationalists a common organisation. The RDA did not aim at a front against France at first (option B), Senghor was not its leader (option C; he founded his own movement in 1948), and France did not ban all political activity (option D). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: it led to the birth of the RDA.
it rallied the political forces in French West Africa against France.
it led to the emergence of Senghor as leader of the French West Africa.
it caused the French administration to ban all political activities in West Africa.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A significant outcome of the Mau Mau Revolt in Kenya was:

*Options as printed:* A) the holding of the Lancaster Conference.   B) expulsion of white settlers from the country.   C) the liberation and independence of Kenya.   D) the devastation of the indigenous economy.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Mau Mau revolt (1952-1960), mainly among the Kikuyu, led the British to declare a state of emergency, which was lifted in 1960. Although it was defeated militarily, it showed that settler rule could not continue, and it speeded up constitutional change: the Lancaster House conferences (1960 and 1962) prepared African majority rule and Kenya became independent in December 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta. Options A and C therefore both describe real consequences, one an immediate step and the other the final result, while white settlers were not expelled (option B). The printed options do not allow a single best key, so the question is left open.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Portuguese unwillingness to grant independence to Angola can be attributed to:

*Options as printed:* A) the dependence on Angolan resources for Portugal's industrial development.   B) the dependence on Portugal by Angola for agricultural and mineral resources.   C) the job opportunities granted to Angolans by the Portuguese government.   D) the inability of Angolans to manage investments made by Portugal.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Portugal, a poor country with a weak economy, treated Angola as an 'overseas province' and relied on its coffee, diamonds, iron and (later) oil, as well as on markets for its goods and settlement for its people; for this reason it resisted independence until the war in Angola (from 1961) and the fall of the dictatorship in Portugal in 1974, and Angola became independent in 1975. Option A states this dependence of Portugal on Angola's resources. Option B, as printed, reverses the direction of dependence (Angola on Portugal) or is badly worded, and options C and D do not explain the policy. Because of the confusing wording of option B the question is left open for self-assessment.

**Intended answer: A (the dependence on Angolan resources for Portugal's industrial development).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
French Equatorial Africa was subjected to the French Neo-colonial policies after independence mainly because:

*Options as printed:* A) their economies were very strong and attractive to the French government.   B) the terms of trade with France at independence were more favourable to the African states.   C) all the former colonies depended on France for manufactured goods and other services.   D) French financial and monetary institutions depended on the former African colonies.
questions.corrige_markdown:
After independence in 1960, the states of former French Equatorial Africa (Chad, Gabon, Congo and Central African Republic) remained tied to France through the CFA franc and the French Treasury, cooperation and defence agreements, French advisers and trading arrangements. This neo-colonial control was possible because their economies were weak and depended on France for manufactured goods, capital, expertise and other services (option C). Their economies were not strong (option A), the terms of trade did not favour them (option B), and option D reverses the dependence as printed (French institutions depending on the former colonies), which makes it false as written and may be a misprint of the intended statement. Because of this defective option, the question is left open for self-assessment.

**Intended answer: C (all the former colonies depended on France for manufactured goods and other services).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The most effective method used to enforce Apartheid in South Africa was:
questions.corrige_markdown: After the National Party victory of 1948, apartheid was enforced mainly through a body of laws backed by police power: the Population Registration Act, Group Areas Act, pass laws, the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act, Bantu Education Act, the Bantustan policy and the Suppression of Communism Act. Marriage bans, school restrictions and mine labour rules (options A, C and D) were only parts of this legal system, and Black labour was in fact heavily used in the mines (option C) and Black children did attend separate, inferior schools (option D). **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: the prevention of marriages between Blacks and Coloured people.
the adoption of stringent Apartheid laws which restrained the Black population.
the refusal of Black labour in the rich mines controlled by the whites.
the prevention of Black children from attending any school in South Africa.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Military coups in Africa since independence have mostly been blamed on:

*Options as printed:* A) Neo-colonialism and imperialism.   B) the absence of parliamentary democracy.   C) persistent deficits in the terms of trade.   D) over expenditure on arms and ammunitions.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Many African states experienced military coups after independence (for example Nigeria and Ghana in 1966). Writers blame a mix of causes: weak and divided political institutions, one-party and personal rule that left no peaceful means of changing governments (the absence of real parliamentary democracy), corruption, ethnic rivalry, economic hardship, the ambitions of army officers, and outside interference (neo-colonialism). Authors differ on which of these is the main cause, and the printed options (A and B above all) cannot be ranked with certainty, so the question is left open.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The main factor that influenced the civil war in Rwanda in the 1990s was:
questions.corrige_markdown: Rwanda's civil war began in October 1990 when the Rwandan Patriotic Front, made up mostly of Tutsi exiles, invaded from Uganda, and it ended in the genocide of April to July 1994 that followed the death of President Habyarimana. It was rooted in the rivalry between the Hutu majority and the Tutsi minority, sharpened by Belgian colonial favouritism towards the Tutsi, the 1959 Hutu revolution and decades of exile and discrimination. Religion (option A) did not divide them, drought (option B) was not the cause, and the RPF sought a return and a share of power, not secession (option C). **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: religious antagonism.
droughts and desertification.
secessionist attempts.
tribalism and ethnicity.

questions.enonce_markdown: The immediate cause of the 1688 English Revolution was:
questions.corrige_markdown: James II, a Catholic, had alarmed Protestants by promoting Catholics, keeping a standing army and bringing the Declaration of Indulgence. His daughter Mary, wife of William of Orange, was Protestant and seemed likely to succeed him. The birth of his son, James Francis Edward, on 10 June 1688 created a Catholic heir and made a Catholic dynasty likely, which pushed leading Englishmen to invite William, who landed at Torbay in November 1688. The standing army and the suppression of the Monmouth Rebellion (1685) were earlier, long-term grievances, and cabinet reshuffles were of little importance. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the raising of a standing army.
vindictive cabinet reshuffles.
the birth of the Prince of Wales.
the brutal suppression of the Monmouth Rebellion.

questions.enonce_markdown: Colonists' rejection of British taxes was based on the argument that:
questions.corrige_markdown: After the Seven Years' War (1756-63) Britain imposed new taxes on the American colonies (the Stamp Act of 1765, the Townshend duties of 1767, the Tea Act of 1773). The colonists objected on principle: they had no representatives in the British Parliament, so it had no right to tax them, 'no taxation without representation'. They did not want to pay French taxes (option B), Britain had in fact fought the war partly in their defence (option C), and the amount of the taxes was not the argument (option D). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: they were not consulted by the British parliament.
they preferred to pay French taxes which were not heavy.
Britain did not help them in the Seven Years War.
the taxes were insignificant to develop America.

questions.enonce_markdown: The Troppau Protocol of 1820 was aimed at:
questions.corrige_markdown: After revolutions broke out in Spain and Naples in 1820, Austria, Prussia and Russia met at the Congress of Troppau (late 1820) and issued the Troppau Protocol, which declared that the great powers had the right to intervene, by force if needed, against any state where a revolution had changed the government. It was used to send Austrian troops to restore the king in Naples in 1821, and Britain refused to support it. Its aim was therefore to suppress revolts, not simply to maintain peace in general (option A), and it was not directed at France (option B) or at pirates (option C). **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: maintaining peace in Europe.
crushing French military ambitions.
checking the Barbary pirates.
suppressing revolts in Europe.

questions.enonce_markdown: The negotiation that led to the signing of the Russo-German Re-insurance Treaty was undertaken mainly because:
questions.corrige_markdown: In 1887 the Dreikaiserbund (alliance of the three emperors) was falling apart because of Austro-Russian rivalry in the Balkans, and Bismarck feared that Russia would turn to France, which would leave Germany facing a war on two fronts. He therefore signed the secret Reinsurance Treaty with Russia in June 1887 to keep Russia from allying with France. It was not renewed in 1890 after Bismarck's fall, and the Franco-Russian alliance followed in the 1890s. France was isolated (not about to attack, option B), it had no rapprochement with Austria-Hungary (option C) and no alliance with Britain yet (option D, the Entente Cordiale dates from 1904). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the prospect of a Franco-Russian Alliance was very high.
France was planning to attack Germany.
Austria-Hungary and France were planning a rapprochement.
France had allied with Britain.

questions.enonce_markdown: An incident in the Balkans that precipitated World War 1 was:
questions.corrige_markdown: Austria-Hungary, which had occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina since 1878, annexed them in 1908, which angered Serbia and Russia and deepened Balkan tension; it is the only printed option that is an actual incident, and it was followed by the Sarajevo assassination of 28 June 1914, the immediate spark (not offered among the options). Pan-Germanism against Pan-Slavism (option A) is a rivalry of ideas and not an incident, and options B and D are not recognised incidents. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the rivalry between Pan-Germanism and Pan-Slavism.
Russia's desire to create a big Bulgarian state.
Austria-Hungary's annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
the nationalist activities of Russia.

questions.enonce_markdown:
German bitterness against the Versailles Treaty of 1919 stemmed from the fact that:

*Options as printed:* A) her military was drastically reduced.   B) she was asked to pay reparations.   C) she lost some of her overseas colonies.   D) she was denied the right to self-determination.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Treaty of Versailles (28 June 1919) took away German territory in Europe and all her overseas colonies, limited her army to 100,000 men and forbade tanks and an air force, made her accept the war-guilt clause, forced her to pay heavy reparations (fixed in 1921), and forbade the union with Austria, so that German-speaking peoples were denied self-determination. All four printed statements are true and cause bitterness, and the question does not say which was the main cause (reparations are most often put first), so the printed question has no single defensible key and is left open.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The structural weakness of the League of Nations was evident in:
questions.corrige_markdown: The League (founded in 1920) needed unanimous agreement in its Council and Assembly, so any one member could block a decision, and it had no army of its own to enforce decisions. This was a flaw in its structure. The absence of the United States and, for some years, of Germany and the USSR (option C) weakened it in membership, and the policy of appeasement (option D) was a policy of states, not a structural feature. The Conference of Ambassadors (option A) was an Allied body outside the League. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: the conflict between the Council and Conference of Ambassadors.
the use of the principle of unanimity in decision making.
the absence of some great powers in the organisation.
the Anglo-French Policy of Appeasement.

questions.enonce_markdown: The Anglo-French Policy of Appeasement contributed to the outbreak of the Second World War because:
questions.corrige_markdown: Britain and France gave way to Hitler's demands (the remilitarisation of the Rhineland in 1936, the Anschluss in 1938, the Munich Agreement of September 1938 and the German seizure of Czechoslovakia in 1939) instead of resisting. This allowed Germany to rearm and strengthen herself and gave Germany and Italy time to prepare for war. Appeasement did not discourage a German-British alliance (option B), and it pushed Stalin towards the Nazi-Soviet Pact of August 1939 rather than towards the Western Powers (option C). The German attack on Poland on 1 September 1939 was Hitler's own decision (option D). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: it gave the aggressors time to mobilise for war.
it discouraged an alliance between Germany and Britain.
it made Russia to form an alliance with the Western Powers.
it precipitated the German attack on Poland.

questions.enonce_markdown: The following were political effects of the Second World War EXCEPT:
questions.corrige_markdown: The war left the United States and the USSR as the two super powers (option A), strengthened nationalist movements in Asia and Africa (option B), and led to the creation of the United Nations Organisation in 1945 (option C). Marshall Aid (the European Recovery Programme of 1948) was an American economic aid programme to rebuild Western Europe, so it is the economic exception. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the rise of Super Powers.
the growth of nationalism.
the creation of the UNO.
the granting of Marshall Aid.

questions.enonce_markdown: The Berlin Crisis of 1948-1949 was a consequence of:
questions.corrige_markdown: In June 1948 the Western powers introduced a new currency, the Deutsche Mark, in their zones and then in West Berlin. Stalin saw this as a step towards a separate West German state and cut road, rail and canal links to West Berlin from 24 June 1948; the Western allies supplied the city by air until the blockade ended in May 1949. The blockade (option B) was the crisis itself, not its cause, disagreement over reparations (option D) was a longer-term source of tension, and the flight of East Germans (option A) became a major issue later, leading to the Berlin Wall in 1961. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the migration of citizens from East Germany.
Soviet blockade of West Berlin.
currency reforms in the western sector of Germany.
disagreement over reparations collection.

questions.enonce_markdown: An important outcome of the Korean War of 1950-53 was that it:
questions.corrige_markdown: The war began in June 1950 with the North Korean invasion of South Korea and ended with the armistice of July 1953. The UN Security Council, with the Soviet delegate absent, authorised a UN force under American command to defend South Korea, the first collective military action of the UN, which showed that it could act where the League of Nations had failed and raised its prestige. The war did not divide China and the USSR, whose alliance was strengthened (option A), Korea stayed divided near the 38th parallel (option C), and the USA and China fought each other, so there was no cooperation (option D). **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: intensified hostility between China and the USSR.
increased the prestige of the UNO.
led to the unification of the two Korean states..
increased cooperation between the USA and China.

questions.enonce_markdown: The most important objective of the United Nations Organisation since its creation has been to:
questions.corrige_markdown: The first purpose stated in Article 1 of the UN Charter (1945) is to maintain international peace and security, and the Security Council was created for that task. Coordination, human rights and disarmament (options A, C and D) are real functions but serve this central goal. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: coordinate the activities of all its members.
promote world peace and security.
promote fundamental human rights.
promote world disarmament.

questions.enonce_markdown: A major handicap to the smooth functioning of the Commonwealth of Nations was seen in :
questions.corrige_markdown: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of independent states with no binding authority, so it works by consensus. Disagreements among members on major issues, such as apartheid in South Africa (which left in 1961), the Rhodesian declaration of independence in 1965 and the Suez crisis of 1956, repeatedly made common action difficult. Dues (option A) are small, membership of other bodies (option B) is not a major obstacle, and the Commonwealth was never meant to have an army (option C). **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the inability by poor states to pay their financial dues.
allegiance of members to other organisations.
absence of a standing army to enforce its decisions.
differences over important issues.

questions.enonce_markdown: The State of Israel has survived since 1948 for the following reasons EXCEPT:
questions.corrige_markdown: Israel was proclaimed on 14 May 1948 and survived the war with its Arab neighbours in 1948-49 and later wars (1956, 1967, 1973). It did so thanks to American and other Western military and financial support (option A), the determination and strong morale of its people and army (option B), and the disunity and rivalries among the Arab states (option C). The Soviet Union backed Arab states such as Egypt and Syria after the early 1950s (Soviet-approved arms from Czechoslovakia reached Israel only briefly in 1948), so continuing Soviet military support is the exception. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Western military support to Israel.
Israel's determination to exist.

questions.enonce_markdown: The Sino-American Detente was necessary in the 1970s mainly because:
questions.corrige_markdown: By the early 1970s both countries had reasons to draw closer: the United States wanted help in ending the Vietnam War and a counterweight to the USSR, while China, after border clashes with the USSR in 1969, wanted security, an end to isolation and access to trade. Kissinger's secret visit (1971), China's seat at the United Nations (1971) and Nixon's visit to Beijing (1972) followed. Taiwan (Formosa) was not hostile to the USA (option B), China did not abandon communism (option C), and South Korea did not press the USA to do this (option D). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: both China and the United States valued the importance of each other.
the government at Formosa had become increasingly hostile to the USA.
the Chinese government was prepared to abandon its extreme communism.
of pressure from the South Korean government on the United States.
